With ⟦p:hosea_1555|Hosea⟧ we come to a new part of the Old Testament. The last twelve books are short prophetic works that Jewish tradition copied together on a single scroll and called simply the Twelve. They are known as the minor prophets only because of their length. Between them they cover about three centuries, from the days when ⟦l:assyria_111|Assyria⟧ dominated the Near East to the years after the return from exile under ⟦l:persia_938|Persia⟧, and they are not arranged in the order in which they were spoken. Hosea stands first, and it belongs among the earliest of them.

⟦p:hosea_1555|Hosea⟧ son of Beeri spoke to the northern kingdom of Israel in the eighth century before Christ. The listener met that kingdom in the books of Kings: the ten tribes that broke away from ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧'s son ⟦p:rehoboam_2412|Rehoboam⟧, with their capital at ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧ and their royal shrines at ⟦l:bethel_202|Bethel⟧ and Dan, where ⟦p:jeroboam_873|Jeroboam⟧ son of ⟦p:nebat_2165|Nebat⟧ set up the golden calves. Unlike Amos, who came up from Judah, Hosea was a man of the north speaking to his own people. His ministry began under a later Jeroboam, Jeroboam son of ⟦p:joash_1633|Jehoash⟧, whose reign of some forty years gave Israel its last great season of strength. Its borders were pushed out almost to where they had been under Solomon, trade flourished, and the shrines were crowded with worshippers.

⟦p:hosea_1555|Hosea⟧ saw a sickness beneath the prosperity. Alongside the Lord, the people were serving ⟦p:baal_573|Baal⟧, the Canaanite storm god who was believed to send the rain and make fields and flocks fertile. Many did not think of this as abandoning the Lord at all. They simply mixed the two on the same hilltops. To Hosea this was adultery, and he describes it in the language of a broken marriage, because his own marriage had become the message. The book opens with it. The Lord tells Hosea to take a prostitute as his wife, and he marries ⟦p:gomer_1329|Gomer⟧. Their children's names are prophecies, and Hosea's costly love for his wayward wife becomes a living picture of the Lord and Israel.

The years that followed were among the darkest in Israel's history. After ⟦p:jeroboam_873|Jeroboam⟧'s death the second book of Kings records a rapid run of murders and usurpers. His son Zechariah, the last of ⟦p:jehu_817|Jehu⟧'s dynasty, was killed after six months. Shallum lasted a month. ⟦p:menahem_1996|Menahem⟧ paid a heavy tribute to the king of ⟦l:assyria_111|Assyria⟧ to keep his throne. His son ⟦p:pekahiah_2300|Pekahiah⟧ was struck down by his officer ⟦p:pekah_2299|Pekah⟧, and Pekah in turn by ⟦p:joshua_1727|Hoshea⟧, the last king of Israel, whose name in Hebrew is the same as the prophet's. All the while Assyria, under ⟦p:tilgath-pilneser_2376|Tiglath-pileser⟧ and then Shalmaneser, was pressing westward, and the kings of ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧ lurched between paying tribute to Assyria and looking to ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧ for help. In the end Hoshea rebelled, Samaria was besieged for three years, and in about seven hundred and twenty-two before Christ the city fell and its people were carried into exile.

⟦p:hosea_1555|Hosea⟧ lived through much of this. The opening line dates his ministry by the kings of Judah from ⟦p:uzziah_375|Uzziah⟧ to ⟦p:hezekiah_1512|Hezekiah⟧, a span of thirty years or more. Most of his words look ahead to the fall of ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧. His contemporaries were Amos, a little earlier, and in Judah, ⟦p:isaiah_617|Isaiah⟧ and Micah.

After the three chapters about his family, the rest of the book is a long collection of oracles, seldom dated and not arranged as a chronicle. The poetry is dense and abrupt. It moves without warning from accusation to grief to tenderness, and it is full of images from farm and household: a stubborn heifer, a half-baked cake, morning mist, a lion, a parent teaching a child to walk. Again and again ⟦p:hosea_1555|Hosea⟧ reaches back into Israel's past, to the exodus, the wilderness and the patriarch ⟦p:israel_682|Jacob⟧. His usual name for the nation is ⟦p:ephraim_1206|Ephraim⟧, after its largest tribe, and Judah appears from time to time, sometimes warned, sometimes set in contrast.

⟦p:hosea_1555|Hosea⟧'s picture of the Lord as a wounded husband would be taken up by ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧ and ⟦p:ezekiel_1237|Ezekiel⟧ more than a century later, and several of his lines are quoted in the New Testament. His words were kept in Judah after the northern kingdom was gone, and the book ends not with ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧'s ruin but with an invitation to return.

The book begins with its date line and then moves straight to the first word the Lord gave ⟦p:hosea_1555|Hosea⟧. It is a command about his own life. He is to take a prostitute as his wife and have children of adultery, because the land itself has played the harlot and departed from the Lord.

He marries ⟦p:gomer_1329|Gomer⟧ daughter of ⟦p:diblaim_1009|Diblaim⟧, and three children follow, each named by the Lord. The first is ⟦p:jezreel_1613|Jezreel⟧, after the valley and town where, nearly a century earlier, ⟦p:jehu_817|Jehu⟧ had seized the throne in a bloodbath and wiped out the house of ⟦p:ahab_113|Ahab⟧. King ⟦p:jeroboam_873|Jeroboam⟧ is Jehu's great-grandson, and the name announces that the dynasty founded in blood will end. The second child, a daughter, is ⟦p:lo-ruhamah_1829|Lo-ruhamah⟧, meaning no compassion. The third is ⟦p:lo-ammi_1827|Lo-ammi⟧, not my people, words that strike at the heart of the covenant.

Yet the chapter does not end there. In its closing lines the names are turned inside out, and a future is promised in which Israel and Judah are gathered together again under one leader.
2:
The story of ⟦p:hosea_1555|Hosea⟧'s household now becomes poetry, and the line between ⟦p:gomer_1329|Gomer⟧ and Israel begins to blur. The Lord speaks as a husband bringing a case against an unfaithful wife, and the children are told to rebuke their mother.

Her lovers are the Baals, the local forms of the god thought to give rain and harvest. The irony is that the grain, the new wine and the oil were the Lord's gifts all along, and Israel has credited them to someone else. So he will take them back and silence her festivals.

Then, midway, the tone changes. Instead of driving her away, the Lord will lead her into the wilderness, where Israel first knew him after ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧, and speak tenderly to her. The ⟦l:valley_of_achor_1196|Valley of Achor⟧, remembered from ⟦p:joshua_1727|Joshua⟧'s day as the valley of trouble, will become a gateway of hope. There is wordplay too: the Hebrew baal also means master, or husband. By the end the children's names are reversed, and the apostle ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ would later hear in these lines a promise reaching even to the Gentiles.
3:
This brief chapter returns to ⟦p:hosea_1555|Hosea⟧'s own story, and now he tells it himself. His wife has gone to another man, and the Lord tells him to go and love her again, as the Lord loves Israel even while they turn to other gods.

⟦p:hosea_1555|Hosea⟧ pays to bring her back, partly in silver and partly in barley. He then sets terms: a long period in which she will belong to no one else, and he will wait.

The meaning follows at once. Israel too must live for many days without king or prince, without sacrifice and the objects of their worship. Only afterwards will they return and seek the Lord their God and ⟦p:david_994|David⟧ their king. Spoken to the north, that last phrase looks for a day when the divided kingdoms are united again under David's line. With this the first part of the book is complete.
4:
From here to the end, the book is a collection of ⟦p:hosea_1555|Hosea⟧'s oracles. The story of the marriage is over, but its language runs through everything that follows.

The first oracle opens like a court case. The Lord has a charge against the people of the land: there is no truth, no loving devotion, and no knowledge of God. The commandments are broken one after another, and even the land mourns.

Much of the blame falls on the priests, whose task was to teach the law. Because they have forgotten it, the people are destroyed for lack of knowledge, and the verdict is blunt: like people, like priest. Worship has moved to the hilltops and the shade of sacred trees, bound up with ritual prostitution. Two shrines are named, ⟦l:gilgal_476|Gilgal⟧ and ⟦l:beth-aven_191|Beth-aven⟧. Beth-aven, house of wickedness, is ⟦p:hosea_1555|Hosea⟧'s scornful name for ⟦l:bethel_202|Bethel⟧, house of God, the royal sanctuary of the north. And here the nation is first called ⟦p:ephraim_1206|Ephraim⟧, the name Hosea will use most often.

The next oracle summons three groups at once: the priests, the house of Israel and the royal household. Leaders who should have guided the people have become a snare at ⟦l:mizpah_809|Mizpah⟧ and a net spread on ⟦l:tabor_1128|Mount Tabor⟧.

Partway through comes a sudden alarm. The ram's horn is to sound in ⟦l:gibeah_466|Gibeah⟧ and the trumpet in ⟦l:ramah_972|Ramah⟧, and the battle cry is to go up in ⟦l:beth-aven_191|Beth-aven⟧, towns of ⟦p:benjamin_463|Benjamin⟧ on the border between Judah and Israel, as though an enemy were already on the march through the borderlands. ⟦p:hosea_1555|Hosea⟧ finds both kingdoms at fault. ⟦p:ephraim_1206|Ephraim⟧'s answer to its troubles is to send to the great king of ⟦l:assyria_111|Assyria⟧, as ⟦p:menahem_1996|Menahem⟧ had done with his tribute. But Assyria cannot heal this wound. The Lord himself is tearing them like a lion, and he will withdraw until they seek him.

The chapter opens with a song of return. Come, it says, let us return to the Lord, for he has torn us and he will heal us. These are the people's own words, a hopeful response to the warnings they have just heard.

The Lord's answer is full of grief. What shall I do with you, he asks ⟦p:ephraim_1206|Ephraim⟧ and Judah, for your loyalty is like a morning mist, like the early dew that vanishes. Their repentance is real in the moment and gone by mid-morning. Then comes one of ⟦p:hosea_1555|Hosea⟧'s best-known lines: the Lord desires mercy, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings. ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ would quote it twice in the Gospel of ⟦p:matthew_1971|Matthew⟧.

The rest of the chapter names specific crimes. ⟦l:gilead_475|Gilead⟧, east of the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧, is tracked with bloody footprints, and bands of priests lie in ambush on the road to Shechem. A brief word to Judah closes the chapter: a harvest is appointed for them too.
7:
⟦p:hosea_1555|Hosea⟧ now takes us into the royal court at ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧, in the years of plots and assassinations after ⟦p:jeroboam_873|Jeroboam⟧'s death. Courtiers flatter the king while they plan his murder. On the king's feast day the princes are inflamed with wine, and their conspiracy smoulders through the night like a baker's oven, until in the morning it blazes up. All their kings fall, the Lord says, and not one of them calls on me. Within about twenty years, four kings of Israel were killed by the men who replaced them.

The second half turns to foreign policy. ⟦p:ephraim_1206|Ephraim⟧ has mixed itself among the nations, and like a cake left unturned on the griddle, it is burnt on one side and raw on the other. Its strength drains away to foreigners, and like a man going grey, it has not noticed. Ephraim is a silly, senseless dove, fluttering first towards ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧ and then towards ⟦l:assyria_111|Assyria⟧. Israel's last kings did exactly that.
8:
The ram's horn sounds again, a warning of attack, and an eagle hovers over the house of the Lord, the land and people as a whole. The danger from ⟦l:assyria_111|Assyria⟧ is coming closer.

The Lord gives his reasons. Israel has made kings without consulting him, a pointed description of the coups of these years. They have made idols of silver and gold, and above all they cling to the calf of ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧, the golden calf at ⟦l:bethel_202|Bethel⟧ that had stood at the heart of the northern kingdom's worship since ⟦p:jeroboam_873|Jeroboam⟧ son of ⟦p:nebat_2165|Nebat⟧. A craftsman made it, the Lord says, and it is not God.

Here is one of ⟦p:hosea_1555|Hosea⟧'s most memorable sayings: they sow the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind. ⟦p:ephraim_1206|Ephraim⟧ has hired lovers among the nations, buying protection with tribute. Then comes a threat that will recur. They will return to ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧. The people once rescued from slavery will lose their freedom again.

This message is spoken at a harvest festival, when the threshing floors were full and the wine was being pressed. ⟦p:hosea_1555|Hosea⟧ interrupts the celebrations: do not rejoice, O Israel, like the nations. The harvest has been treated as ⟦p:baal_573|Baal⟧'s gift, and soon there will be no feasts at all. The chapter gives a rare glimpse of how ⟦p:hosea_1555|Hosea⟧ himself was received. The prophet is called a fool, the inspired man insane, and snares are laid on his path.

Then he reaches back into Israel's history. The Lord found Israel like grapes in the wilderness, a delight, but at ⟦l:baal-peor_145|Baal-peor⟧, on the edge of the promised land, they gave themselves to a foreign god. The days of ⟦l:gibeah_466|Gibeah⟧, the dreadful crime at the end of Judges, are recalled, and so is ⟦l:gilgal_476|Gilgal⟧. The chapter's last words are hard: they will be wanderers among the nations.

Israel is pictured as a luxuriant vine, and the image becomes an accusation. The more the land prospered, the more altars and sacred pillars the people built.

A time is coming, ⟦p:hosea_1555|Hosea⟧ says, when they will admit they have no king, and that a king could not have saved them. The calf of ⟦l:beth-aven_191|Beth-aven⟧, their pride, will be carried off to ⟦l:assyria_111|Assyria⟧ as tribute to the great king, and its priests will mourn it. ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧'s king will be swept away like a twig on the water.

Once more the past is called as a witness: since the days of ⟦l:gibeah_466|Gibeah⟧, Israel has sinned. Then the farm images return. ⟦p:ephraim_1206|Ephraim⟧ is a heifer that likes the easy work of threshing and will now be yoked to the plough. In the middle of the warnings comes a call to sow righteousness and break up the unploughed ground, because there is still time to seek the Lord. Its closing lines recall Shalman's destruction of Beth-arbel, an atrocity the first hearers knew well.
11:
After so much accusation, this chapter opens in a different voice. The Lord speaks not as a husband but as a parent. When Israel was a child, he says, I loved him, and out of ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧ I called my son. He remembers teaching ⟦p:ephraim_1206|Ephraim⟧ to walk, holding them by the arms, bending down to feed them.

The memory makes the rebellion all the more painful, and for a moment judgement seems to be the last word. But then the Lord's heart turns within him. How could I give you up, ⟦p:ephraim_1206|Ephraim⟧, he asks. How could I make you like ⟦l:admah_27|Admah⟧ and ⟦l:zeboiim_1244|Zeboiim⟧, two towns overthrown with ⟦l:sodom_1107|Sodom⟧ and ⟦l:gomorrah_489|Gomorrah⟧. For I am God, and not a man.

The chapter closes with the Lord roaring like a lion, and his children coming home trembling from ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧ and ⟦l:assyria_111|Assyria⟧ like birds returning to their nests. ⟦p:matthew_1971|Matthew⟧'s Gospel would later hear the line about the son called out of Egypt in the childhood of ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧.

⟦p:ephraim_1206|Ephraim⟧ feeds on the wind. The chapter opens with the double game of Israel's last years, a treaty with ⟦l:assyria_111|Assyria⟧ while olive oil is sent to ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧ to win its favour. The second book of Kings records that King ⟦p:joshua_1727|Hoshea⟧ did just this, sending to So king of Egypt while still bound to Assyria.

Then ⟦p:hosea_1555|Hosea⟧ turns to the nation's ancestor. ⟦p:israel_682|Jacob⟧, whose other name was Israel, grasped his brother's heel in the womb, wrestled with God, wept and sought his favour, and met him at ⟦l:bethel_202|Bethel⟧. He fled to ⟦l:aram_82|Aram⟧ and tended sheep to win a wife. Hosea holds up the patriarch's story as a mirror: the nation has inherited Jacob's grasping, but not his seeking.

The merchant with dishonest scales who boasts that no one can find fault in him is ⟦p:ephraim_1206|Ephraim⟧ itself. Against this the Lord sets his own long history with them, from ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧ onwards, and the prophets he sent, beginning with ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧, by whom Israel was brought out and preserved.
13:
The end of the northern kingdom is very near in this chapter. It begins with ⟦p:ephraim_1206|Ephraim⟧'s past greatness, when its word made others tremble. But through ⟦p:baal_573|Baal⟧ it died, and now the people make silver idols and kiss the calves.

A sequence of fierce images follows. They will vanish like morning mist, like chaff from the threshing floor, like smoke from a window. The Lord, who knew them in the wilderness, will meet them like a lion, a leopard and a bear robbed of her cubs. The kings they demanded cannot save them. In my anger I gave you a king, the Lord says, and in my wrath I took him away. Israel's last kings were removed one by one, and ⟦p:joshua_1727|Hoshea⟧ himself ended his reign in an Assyrian prison.

A line about death and Sheol follows that the apostle ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ would later echo in his great chapter on the resurrection. Here it stands amid judgement, and the chapter ends with ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧ facing the horrors of siege.
14:
The book ends with an invitation. After all the warnings, ⟦p:hosea_1555|Hosea⟧ calls Israel to return to the Lord, and even gives them the words to say. They are to ask him to take away their iniquity, and to renounce the three things they have trusted: ⟦l:assyria_111|Assyria⟧, the horses of war, and the idols made by their own hands.

The Lord's answer is the gentlest passage in the book. He will heal their unfaithfulness and love them freely. Earlier, Israel's loyalty vanished like the dew; now the Lord himself will be like the dew to Israel. The images come from the north's own landscape: the lily, the olive tree, the cedars and the wine of ⟦l:lebanon_720|Lebanon⟧.

The final line is addressed to anyone wise enough to understand, as though to the readers who would study this scroll in Judah long after ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧ was gone. The ways of the Lord are right, it says, and the righteous walk in them. Next among the Twelve comes Joel, and a land stripped bare by locusts.
